Vadhūla Śrautasūtra 8: On the Piling of the Fire Altar (Agnicayana)

"M*" in this transcription corresponds to M’s *anunāsika* script "guṃ". <1> Preparatory rites: 1. the *saṃbhāras*; 2. the introductory *iṣṭi* of the *caru* (which is not found in Baudh.); 3. the *sāvitra* offering. ÊÊ[K1,52a; K4,52a; M.234-5]
cf. Anvākhyāna <1>–<4> {C No. 102, 103a.} p. 234:6–7 (on certain formulas), cf. AO 4, No. 56, p. 163.

[When about to collect the materials for the fire-pan (*ukhā*), he collects the materials: a horse and a donkey, two ropes, a spade, large offering-spoons (*sruk*), small offering-spoons (*sruva*), a vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), a water-pitcher, a hundred-measure weight (*śatamāna*), a mound of anthill earth, clay from a pit, a cord, a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), two lotus leaves, the hair of a black antelope skin and the hair of a goat, pebbles, potsherds, and a decoction of *parṇa* leaves... (17? for which he prepares the sacrificial porridge (*caru*).

When [the offering] has been poured out, he recites the *prāṇagraha* formulas and the *pṛśni* verses. When it is near [to completion], he recites the *apānagraha* formulas, the *pṛśni* verses, and the *daśahotṛ* formula.

For this [offering], the two butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*) are the *vārtraghnas*. The invitatory verse (*puro'nuvākyā*) for the oblation is: "Two oceans... (TS 3.2.2.1), ending with "...they cross over another by means of a bridge.

At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering. The two concluding offerings (*saṃyājye*) are in the *triṣṭubh* meter. He makes his own offering following the continuous stream of the Hotṛ’s offering.
The ritual act is accomplished; this sacrifice comes to a conclusion. When it has been concluded, he immediately offers a *caru* oblation for Brahman.
The procedure for this [second] sacrifice is the same as that of the previous one; the *daśahotṛ* formula itself serves as the *hotṛ*.

With the verse, “Brahma was born first” (4.2.8d,1), [he offers] the oblation... up to “the opening of that which exists from the beginning” (ibid.). The *yājyā* is: “The calf of the *virāj*s, the bull of riches, the multiform one has entered the intermediate space; him they honor with hymns—the calf who is Brahman, magnifying him with Brahman” (TB 2.8.8.9w,1; cf. AS(S) 13.1.33). (ibid.)
"Let the four quarters proceed, O Agnis," he says as he places the *upaśayī* (the lying-down fire). "May this sacrifice of ours lead [us], [may it lead] the oblations," [he says] until the end.

At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he offers the two *triṣṭubh* *saṃyājyā* verses. He offers the oblation following the continuity of the Hotṛ's [recitation]. The rite is successfully accomplished; this sacrifice comes to a conclusion.
At the time for the northern altar (uttaravedi), they dig a well corresponding to this [southern] altar; into it they place earth suitable for the pit (karuṇīyā mṛd);
to its south, they set down a water-pitcher.

To the west of that [spot] he places the mound of the anthill. To the west of that stands a man, instructed [to hold it], with two verses beginning, "In me I first take Agni" (5.7.9.1a), the two Adhvaryus take the fire into themselves: "For the increase of wealth... has gone forth" (ibid., the last two verses).

With the words, “O Agni, those logs of thine” (5.7.8a,1), he mutters the *svayañciti* formula; with the words, “The abodes which [thou knowest], knowing them” (ibid., to the end), he takes four spoonfuls of ghee and offers it.

With the words, “May Agni hear my call with the log” (1.3.13g,1), he performs the *anuvitti* offering in the Āhavanīya fire; with the words, “May the waters hear my call, svāhā! (ibid., to the end, with *svāhā*), he offers.
Furthermore, he takes four portions and offers them,

reciting the eight *sāvitra* verses beginning with "yuñjānaḥ prathamam manaḥ" (4.1.1a–h), making the final verse a *yajus*: "rcā stomaṃ samardhaya" (4.1.1i, 1), ending with "gāyatreṇa rathantaraṃ bṛhad gāyatravartani svāhā" (ibid., with *svāhā*).
With the four [formulas], beginning with “At the impulse of the god Savitṛ” (4.1.1k,1), he takes up the spade {cf.
Anvākhyāna on 4.1.1a-h, Caland, *Vierte Mittheilung*, 103a-b (pp. 223–226)}.
<2> Procession to the clay shed; the clay pit (1). [K1,52a8–; K4,52a7–11 M.235–6]

With four [verses] he takes up the spade: "By the arms of the Aśvins, by the hands of Pūṣan, with the Gāyatra [meter]. (cf. Akh.<5>; line 6–9, cf. Caland, *Dritte Mitteilung*, No. 57, p. 163; line 1ff., cf. Caland, *Vierte Mitteilung*, No. 104, pp. 226–7).

With the formula, "I take [thee] with the *chandas* of the Aṅgirases; thou art a spade, thou art a woman; I take thee with the *anuṣṭubh* metre of the Aṅgirases" (4.1.1k, 2n), he takes the horse's halter with the verse, "They have grasped this halter of Order" (4.1.2a, 1);
he takes the donkey's [halter] silently; and [he takes it] with the verse, "In former times... Saramā, crying out" (ibid., last part).
With the words, “Run forward, O steed! (4.1.2b,1), he addresses the horse; with “The most excellent womb” (ibid., final part), [he addresses] the donkey;

with “Yoke the donkey, you two! (4.1.2c,1), [he addresses] the donkey; and with “In this journey, O you who possess bull-like wealth, [bring] Indra for our aid” (ibid., 2 and d), he fastens the two reins together.

With “Come forward, hastening, trampling down” (4.1.2e,1), they proceed with the horse in front, and silently with the donkey behind; [the latter is addressed] with “Away from the curses of Rudra, come toward us with song” (ibid., 2 and f).

When the man has been instructed with the word "kvetha," he asks; [the Adhvaryu] says, "We go to fetch Agni Purīṣya in the manner of Aṅgiras" (4.1.2g). With the words, "I choose strength for thee" (5.2.1.4–5), and "We shall carry Agni Purīṣya in the manner of Aṅgiras" (4.1.2h), he worships the ant-hill. When he perceives the clay from the Karuṇīya site, he causes him to recite, "Agni has looked along the forefront of the dawns" (4.1.2k,1), and [he continues] until the end with, "He has stretched along the days" (ibid.).

Having arrived with the verse, "May the steed come upon the path" (4.1.2 l, 1), he causes the horse to step forward toward the east with its right hoof upon the clay of the southern shoulder of the altar, with the verse, "May he crush the enemies" (ibid., to the end).
Having stepped upon the earth with the verse, "O steed, having stepped upon the earth" (4.1.2 m, 1), he then turns back westward with that same [verse], "Seeking Agni, may we... (ibid., to the end).

With the mantra, "Heaven is your back" (4.1.2n,1), he wipes its back; with "Earth is your seat... may the enemies who attack be held down; you are the holder, so-and-so," (ibid., to the end—though the last five words are unidentified), the sacrificer meditates upon whomsoever he hates; then, with the two mantras beginning with "Step forth" (4.1.2o-p?), he causes it to step out.
[The mantra corrected in 4.1.2n contains some additional words; this is another instance where the Vādhūla tradition may possess a *saṃhitā* different from that of the TS.
<3> The clay pit (2):
With the two verses beginning with "utkrāma," he causes [the animal] to step out, ending with "for great good fortune... the highest" (TS 4.1.2o.2–p).

He pours out water with the words, "O divine waters, flow forth" (4.1.2q,1). He takes four spoonfuls [of ghee] with the words, "Honey-sweet, full of fruit" (ibid., last part). For him, he recites: "Offering oblation with ghee to the god Agni, who is to be approached, his imperishable, bright radiance shines among the gods" (?; cf. 4.1.5g,2 & TB 2.6.16.2; BSS 10.3:3.2; Caland No. 47, p. 161 = KS 344).

Sitting facing east, he places gold on the two words of the verse, “I kindle Agni with mind and with ghee” (4.1.2.1), and offers an oblation. Then, saying, “To him looking toward us, the knower, svāhā!

(ibid., the last word, with ‘svāhā’), he takes another fourfold-drawn portion of ghee. For that, he recites: “May we sit near you with reverence, offering ghee-oblations—the immortal one with flaming hair, the bright one, who is borne abundantly in the ladle. (Cf. Caland, *Dritte M*, No. 48, p. 161). [K4, 52b]

Sitting facing west, having placed gold near the two words “I sprinkle thee with speech and with ghee” (4.1.2.1), he offers [the oblation] with the formula ending in “*svāhā*”: “Rejoicing in the *rakṣas*-slayer, *svāhā*” (ibid., to the end).

With the three verses beginning, “The sage, lord of booty” (4.1.2t,1), he draws a line around the clay for the *karuṇī* with a wooden shovel; with the *gāyatrī* verse, “Agni [accepts] the oblations... of the donor” (4.1.2t, to the end); with the *anuṣṭubh* verse, “Around thee, O Agni, as a fortress... protect us” (4.1.2v,1); and with the *triṣṭubh* verse, “Thou, O Agni, by the days... art born pure” (4.1.2w,1).

With the two [formulas], "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ" (4.1.3a,1) and "With the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I dig thee from the earth in the manner of Aṅgiras; I dig thee, O Agni, full of light" (4.1.3a to the end and 4.1.3b), he digs the clay for the *karuṇī* with a wooden shovel.
Then, with "Thou art the back of the waters" (4.1.3c,1), he takes a lotus leaf, [reciting] "Widely extending, thou shalt bear Agni; thou art the most imperishable" (4.1.3c,2).
He spreads this [clay] with the words, “Growing” (ibid., 3), and expands it with, “Spread wide with great abundance” (ibid., 4).

He then covers it with a black antelope skin using the formula, “You two are a shield and you two are armor” (4.1.3d, 1), with the neck of the skin pointing eastward and the hair facing upward, saying, “Unpierced, abundant, full of soil” (ibid., to the end). With the formula, “Thou art full of soil, the bearer of all” (4.1.3f, 1), he first takes a lump of clay from the half of the black antelope skin with a wooden shovel, saying, “Atharvan churned thee forth, O Agni” (ibid., to the end).

"O Agni, from the lotus-leaf, you—" (4.1.3g,1)—this is the second [verse]. "Atharvan churned you forth from the head of the universe, O priest" (ibid., to the end). "And you, the seer Dadhyañc—" (4.1.3h,1)—this is the third [verse]. "The son kindled you, the destroyer of forts" (ibid., to the end). "And you, Pāthya the bull—" (4.1.3i,1)—this is the fourth [verse]: "He kindled you, the greatest slayer of Dasyus, in battle after battle" (ibid., to the end).

With the four subsequent *triṣṭubh* verses beginning with "Sit down, O Hotṛ," he either carries [the fire] or consecrates it; for a Brāhmaṇa, he should collect [the fire] with the preceding *gāyatrī* verses, and for a Rājanya, with the *triṣṭubh* verses.
With the verse "May you two, finding the light, be auspicious," he covers it from above with a lotus leaf;
and with the verse "The two joined by the *śamī* tree, with their breast—unfailing... (etc., to the end).
With the verse, "Unbind the earth" (2.4.8f,1; 3.5.5d; cf. 2.4.10.3), he pours a water-pot into this pit, [reciting] "Break this—release the skin-bag" (ibid., to the end).
[4] Clay-hollow (3): The return procession.
With the formula, "Gently for you, Vāyu" (4.1.4a,1), he stirs it up, [reciting] "Mātariśvan... O Goddess, let there be *vaṣaṭ* for you" (ibid., to the end).

With the verse, "Well-born together with light" (4.1.4b,1), he ties on the black antelope skin; with "A shelter, a protection, O radiant one" (ibid., to the end), and with the two verses beginning "Arise, O you of fair sacrifice" (4.1.4c–d), he stands up; with "Hither, we invoke the goddess... (4.1.4c,2–d), [he proceeds];
with the single verse, "Born as the embryo of the two worlds, O Agni" (4.1.4e,1), he steps forward; and with "O Agni, beautiful, distributed... bellowing over the cows" (ibid., to the end).

He touches the donkey with the words, "Be firm, O you of strong limbs" (4.1.4f,1); [he touches] the horse with "Be swift, O racer, O steed" (ibid.,2); he settles the donkey with "Be broad, be easy to mount" (ibid.,3); and he stands by the settled [horse] with "O carrier of Agni’s soil" (ibid.
to the end), and with "Be auspicious to creatures, [and to those that are human... to the trees]" (4.1.4g,1 to the end).
With the verse, "Let the vigorous steed go forward, neighing loudly" (4.1.4h,1), they proceed with the horse in front;

with "The braying, flying donkey" (4.1.4h,2), [they proceed] with the donkey behind. He follows with the mantra, "Bearing Agni Purīṣya" (4.1.4h,3). [The officiant recites: "Do not fall away from life... O Agni, come for the feast! Order is truth, order is truth" (4.1.4h,4–5).
"What are you carrying?"—thus the man, having been instructed, asks. "We are bearing Agni Purīṣya like Aṅgiras," he replies. "I choose your vigor. (4.1.2.i) Thus [he speaks].

With the mantra, "O plants, receive this fire" (4.1.4l,1), he consecrates the plants spread out to the north of the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra, "Coming, do not strike [it]; may it be auspicious" (ibid., to the end).
With the mantra, "O plants, rejoice in him" (4.1.4m,1), he brings it down with the mantra, "[She] rich in flowers has sat down upon me" (ibid., to the end).

With the verse, “All have magnified Indra” (4.6.3m,1; cf. 5.4.6.5; #TB2.7.15.5; #TB2.7.16.3), he releases the horse toward the north. With the verse, “Him whose expanse is the ocean, whom songs celebrate, the best of charioteers among charioteers, the true lord of spoils, the master” (4.6.3m, to the end), they lead the donkey after him.
[Then follows the preparation, fumigation, and baking of the *ukhā* vessel.
They bring his wives;

when they have arrived, he loosens [the garment] with the verse, “With wide radiance” (4.1.5a,1), and with “Upon the earth” (ibid., to the end), and with the three verses beginning “O Waters, you are indeed the source of bliss” (4.1.5b,1–d), he sprinkles [her] with a decoction of *parṇa* leaves, using the formula, “Lead us to strength... and give birth to us” (4.1.5b,2–4.1.5d).
With the verse, "O Mitra, having united the earth" (4.1.5e,1), he mixes [the clay] with pebbles and potsherds;

with "The earth and the all-pervading one" (ibid., to the end), and with "I unite thee for freedom from disease, for offspring" (4.1.5f,1), he mixes it with the other ingredients; and with "May all the gods, belonging to all men, unite thee with the Anuṣṭubh metre, like Aṅgiras" (ibid., to the end).
Having measured out the clay with the formula, "Thou art the head of Makha" (4.1.5l), he forms a lump;
with the formula, "Ye two are the feet of the sacrifice" (4.1.5m), he supports [the lump] with his two thumbs;
in this very manner, he makes four lumps.

With the words, “The Rudras, having gathered the earth” (4.1.5g,1), he gives the first lump to his wife; she makes a fire-pan (*ukhā*) from it. He consecrates it with the verse, “They have kindled the great light—it has shone” (ibid., to the end), and with the formula, “May the Vasus fashion you” (4.1.5n1,1), followed by: “By the Gāyatrī metre, in the manner of Aṅgiras, you are the earth; you are firm. Bestow upon me offspring, increase of wealth, lordship over cattle, heroic vigor, and kinsmen for the sacrificer” (4.1.5n1,2+n5). [This refers to the lump] when it has been mixed together.
With the words, “May the Vasus fashion you” (4.1.5h), a second time with “May the Rudras fashion you” (?—this is not attested in the Yajurveda; cf.
ṬB 2.6.7d, 3–4), and with “May the Rudras fashion you” (4.1.5n2,1), he consecrates [the brick], saying:
“By the Triṣṭubh metre, like Aṅgiras; you are the intermediate region; you are firm, supporting the earth” (4.1.5n2, to the end + n5).

With the third verse, "Śinīvālī with beautiful braids" (4.1.5i,1), and [the verse] "The Adityas fashion you with white turbans on their hands" (4.1.5i, to the end), he consecrates [the vessel] with the mantra: "By the Jagatī metre, like Aṅgiras; you are the sky, you are firm—for the measuring" (4.1.5n3, to the end + n5).

"Let him fashion the fire-pan with skill"—this is the fourth [verse]. "May the embryo come forth by means of the two arms" (*ibid.* to the end). "May all the gods belonging to Vaiśvānara fashion you"—with this he follows [the action], with the *ānuṣṭubh* metre: "Thou art the quarters, like Aṅgiras; thou art firm; bestow upon me offspring, increase of wealth, lordship over cattle, heroic vigor, and kinsmen for the sacrificer. (4.1.5n4–5)

He makes this very fire-pan (*ukhā*) with three elevations, nine corners, and four breasts; it is fashioned in three ways, for there are three sets of three upright corners. Upon one of these corners, he winds a cord four times, saying:
"May Aditi grasp your opening" (4.1.5p,1). Then he makes the opening above, saying: "With the *pāṅkta* metre, in the manner of Aṅgiras" (4.1.5p, to the last).
Having said, "Having made this great pan" (4.1.5q,1), he places it down, saying: "The earthen vessel for the sake of milk" (ibid., to the last).

He silently makes the other fire-pan; they cause [the clay] to settle, they wash it with cleansing waters, and with purchased bamboo stalks and smooth stones, he thinks it has settled. Then, intending to fumigate it, he gathers the materials: horse-dung, cow-dung, *brunba* grass, dried grass, wood, and the milk of a cow and a goat. To the north of the hall, they dig a four-cornered pit.

Having brought fire from another source into that enclosed space and having kindled seven horse-hair tufts, he throws one by one into the cauldron with the formula, “May the Vasus fumigate thee with the Gāyatrī metre, like Aṅgiras! (4.1.6a1,1);
then he throws [the remaining ones] into the other cauldron silently, with the formulas, “...may the Rudras fumigate thee... may Varuṇa fumigate thee, like Aṅgiras! (4.1.6a1 to the end, a2–a7).

With the words, "Aditi, thee" (4.1.6b,1), he digs into the pit already dug with a wooden shovel; with the words, "O goddess, accompanied by all the gods, in the dwelling-place of the earth—O pit" (ibid., to the end), having spread the cooking materials over the pit, he places the fire-pan (ukhā) with the words, "The wives of the gods, thee" (4.1.6c,1); [and] with the words, "O goddesses, accompanied by all the gods, may they place thee, O pan" (ibid., to the end).

Having placed the other [pot] silently, having covered it with the cooking-vessels (*śrapaṇa*), he kindles it with the mantra, "May the Dhiṣaṇās thee... (4.1.6d1,1), ending with "...kindle thee, O Ukhā" (ibid.). He cooks it with the mantra, "May the Gnas thee... (4.1.6d2,1), ending with "...cook thee, O Ukhā" (ibid.). He bakes it with the mantra, "May the Varūtris thee... (4.1.6d3,1?), ending with "...bake thee, O Ukhā" (ibid.).
He cooks [the clay] with the mantra, "O Janayā, thee"; he cooks with, "O divine vessels, may you all cook the cauldron (ukhā)";

and he worships it with, "O Mitra, cook this cauldron. With the mantra, "May this [cauldron] bestow upon me glory and most wonderful fame," he should neither breathe upon it nor cast his shadow over it. He gazes at it with the same friendly formula, "This [earth], by its greatness, [reaches] heaven."

When he considers [the earth] fumigated, he then scatters the embers from the spade with the mantra, "May the god Savitṛ scatter thee" (ibid. i,1), and with "The fair-handed one, with fair fingers, with fair strength" (ibid., to the end). He causes her to settle with "Not falling upon the earth" (4.1.6k,1), and with "Fill the regions and the quarters" (ibid.
k,2). He raises her up with "Arise, become great" (ibid. k,3), and with "Stand upright, thou art firm" (ibid. k,4, to the end).

He places [the first vessel] silently into the pit of the well; having drawn out the other [vessel], he places it into the very same pit of the well. With the formula, "May the Vasus purify you" (TS 4.1.6.1), he curdles it with goat's milk. With the formulas, "With the Gāyatrī metre, O Aṅgiras," and "With the Anuṣṭubh metre, O Aṅgiras" (ibid., to the end), he causes it to overflow with cow's milk silently.
Silently, having boiled the other [mixture] with goat’s milk, he causes it to overflow with cow’s milk alone; he places the fumigated and boiled *ukhā* [pot] down. [This is the *Traidhātavīya-iṣṭi*.]

This *iṣṭi* is found only in the *Vadhūlasūtra*; cf. *Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 2.4.11 and Caland, *Vierte Mitteilung*, No. 107, p. 229. Regarding the *traidhātavīya-iṣṭi*, cf. *Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 2.4.11–12 and Caland’s “*Unchopfer*,” No. 178; *Āpastamba Śrautasūtra* 19.27.15–21 (Vājapeya), 19.11.22–23.1 (Vājapeya), 20.8.4, 20.23.5 (Aśvamedha), and 22.15.2 (Ahīna). Regarding the *tārpya*, cf. Caland on *Āpastamba Śrautasūtra* 18.5.7.

From this point, the sacrifice is the *traidhātavīya-iṣṭi*. Its materials (*saṃbhārāḥ*) are: gold, a milch-cow, a *tārpya* garment, two lotuses (*puṇḍarīke*), rice and barley, and twelve potsherds (*kapālāni*). They gird [the sacrificial post].

Having arranged the sacrificial implements and having carried forward the water, he offers the Traidhātavīya sacrifice. With the formula, "By the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I pour thee out, acceptable to Indra and Viṣṇu," he pours four handfuls of rice;
in the same way, four handfuls of barley; and in the same way, four handfuls of rice. Once the rice has been poured out, he recites the *prāṇa* formulas.
Having released his speech at the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviskṛt*), he places twelve potsherds face upwards. They pound the rice grains together with the husked barley;
they grind the rice grains alone, and having mixed the flour of the rice grains with that of the barley, he forms two balls.
He places one of the two [pans] on the fire; he causes it to take on a crust. Upon that, he places the barley-meal; he causes it to take on a crust. Upon that, he places the rice-meal;
he causes it to take on a crust. He makes each subsequent layer larger than the preceding one. He covers it with ashes.
This cake for Indra and Viṣṇu, prepared on twelve potsherds and consisting of three layers, is now cooking.

When this has been boiled, he carries away the *stambayajus*, encloses the altar (*vedi*), and mutters the *karaṇa* formula; the ritual action is accomplished until the spreading of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).

Once the *barhis* has been spread, having saturated the four ends of the cloth with clarified butter, he spreads that fourfold cloth over the *barhis* with its fringes pointing eastward, and covers it with a silken garment (*tārpya*).
Upon that [altar], he lays the enclosing sticks (paridhi), places two fuel-sticks (samidh) upon them, and having caused [the sacrificer] to recite over the enclosing sticks, he yokes the fire.

Having returned, he places the *puṇḍarīka* ladle crosswise; upon the two crosswise [ladles], he places the *prastara* bundle, and upon the *prastara*, the *juhū* and the other two ladles (*upabhṛt* and *dhruvā*) wrapped in cloth.

He should not set down the *sruva* ladle on top after moving it about; rather, once the *sruva* has been placed nearby, he recites the *apānagrahas*, the *daśahotṛ*, and the invitatory verse (*anuvāka*) for the fire being kindled: "O Agni, with thy protections... The Hotṛ makes the two *dhāyyā* verses consisting of the *uṣṇih* and *kakubh* meters: "With [thy] heroic deeds he overcomes, through acts of strength, he whose friendship thou hast protected."

With the verse, "The *kakubh* for the *hotṛ*, the two *kakubhs* for the *hotṛ*; the *anuṣṭubh* for the reciter, the *uṣṇih* for the vessel; offer and serve! he releases this [ladle]. With the threefold verse, "O Agni, you who have three stations, O powerful one," he concludes.

When the *sāmidhenī* verses have been recited with the formula "Three are yours," having poured the *āghāra* libation with the *sruva* spoon, he says, "O *āgnīdh*, cleanse the fires thrice each. Having crossed over without touching the two offering-ladles (*sruc*), and having anointed the *dhruvā* ladle and set it down, he chooses the *pravara*.

The Hotṛ, having been impelled, sits down with the offering-ladle... (10) Having performed the *prayāja* offerings and stepped across, he bastes the *dhruvā* vessel with clarified butter as the oblation; then he sacrifices from the *upabhṛt* for the two *ājyabhāga* portions. While spreading a base of butter and cutting portions, he cuts portions from all the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśas*) from both the rear and the front, bringing them together; he bastes them and anoints them back.

He recites: “May speech be auspicious through action... (15). At the sacrifice, he says, “May you two be victorious and prosper. When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he offers the oblation. He says, “Recite for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt,” while spreading the underlayer and cutting portions. He offers with the verse, “Three times his... (RV 4.1.7). Regarding the *sāmidhenī* verses (cf. Caland, Fourth Communication, No. 110, p. 233; cf. Akh <8>, <9>):
from this point on, he immolates an animal dedicated to Prajāpati—a hornless goat with testicles.
Its ritual procedure is well-established up to the *sāmidhenī* verses.

Regarding his *sāmidhenī* verses, there is this deliberation: these are fifteen, or these are seventeen. If he were to perform twenty-one [verses] in a continuous sequence (*parācī*), these would be the eleven *sāmidhenīs*, and the ten beginning with "May the months, O Agni, and the seasons increase thee" (4.1.7a,1) would constitute the twenty-first in that continuous sequence.

Now, if one should perform twenty-four [verses] in the *parācī* manner, these same [verses] constitute the twenty-one *sāmidhenī*s; the two *dhāyyā*s are the *pṛthupājavatī*s. One should make the twenty-fourth *dhāyyā* the verse beginning with "The splendor of him whose sight is like that of a hawk" (TB 2.4.8.1). And these [verses] ending with "As wealth for the hero, at the head of the sacrifice, may he take heed" (ibid. constitute the twenty-four *parācī*s.

Now, if he should perform twenty-four verses in the *aparācī* manner, he should omit these three *dhāyyā*s, namely this one: "Recite the offering-prayer, serve [the gods]" (*ā juhota duvasyata*). He should likewise omit them from among the *sāmidhenī*s; there are ten of one kind and ten of another, making thirty. Of these, the first is a *triṣṭubh* and the last is a *triṣṭubh*. These are the twenty-four *aparācī*s; however, he should recite only seventeen.

This being established, when the *sāmidhenī* verses have been recited, he pours the *āghāra* libation with the *sruva* spoon mentally, as it is self-evident; with the verse, "In the beginning, the Golden Germ (Hiraṇyagarbha) came into being" (4.1.8.1), he pours the subsequent one with the two *sruc* ladles, ending with "we shall worship the Creator of all that exists" (ibid.). The ritual procedure is thus accomplished: he calls for the *āśrāvaṇa*, the *pratyāśrāvaṇa* is made, the *hotṛ* sits down, and being impelled, he takes up the two *sruc* ladles.
He performs the *prayāja* offerings. With the words, "His fuel-sticks (*samidh*) rise upward" (4.1.8a,1), he performs these *hotṛprī* offerings;

with these verses he sacrifices. With "The bright, upward-pointing flames of the Son... (at the end of the same section), he sacrifices to the *samidhs*. With "O Tanūnapāt" (4.1.8b,1)—that is, "Tanūnapāt"—he sacrifices to Tanūnapāt. With "The Asura [is anointed] with ghee" (at the end of the same section), and "Delighted, you reach the sacrifice with honey" (4.1.8c,1), he releases [the offering].

He sacrifices to these Nārāśaṃsa cups with the verse, “This one comes seeking shade” (4.1.8d,1), and he sacrifices to the *iḍā* with the words, “Exulting in power and ghee, in the offerings” (at the end of the same).

He sacrifices to the *barhis* with the words, “May he worship the greatness of this Agni” (4.1.8e,1), and with the words, “May he, the delightful one, bestow [bliss] upon us” (at the end of the same).
He sacrifices to the Doors with the words, “The divine Doors” (4.1.8f,1), and with the words, “All [gods], following him, [enter] as they fly” (at the end of the same).
With the formula, "Te asya" (4.1.8g,1), he sacrifices to them with the verse, "The two divine women [attend] the sacrifice" (ibid., to the end).
With the formula, "The two divine Hotṛ-priests" (4.1.8h,*1), he sacrifices to the two Hotṛ-priests with the verse, "Upright [is] the sacrifice, the well-offered" (ibid., to the end).
With the formula, "The three goddesses" (4.1.8i,1), he sacrifices to them with the verse, "This sacred grass, being praised" (ibid., to the end).

With the verse, "Then the *turīpa*... (4.1.8k,1), he sacrifices to Tvaṣṭṛ with the verse, "The wonderful one among many, Tvaṣṭṛ is well-disposed toward us... (ibid., to the end). With the verse, "O Lord of the Forest... (4.1.8l,1), he sacrifices to Vanaspati with the verse, "Release it, O generous one... may he grant it... (ibid., to the end). With the call, "O Agni Jātavedas, pronounce *svāhā*... (4.1.8m,1), he performs the secondary sacrifice (*pariyajati*) of the omentum (*vapā*) by means of the *svāhākṛti* formula, ending with, "...may they enjoy the offering for Indra" (ibid., to the end).

"The rite succeeds through the omentum; therefore, recite for Prajāpati as the omentum and fat of the goat are being cut. Having thus spoken, while tearing the omentum with the *sruva* spoon, he recites: "He who breathes... (4.1.8o,1), ending with "...to him we shall pay homage" (*nimiṣato... vidhema*). This is the [formula].

"O Śrauṣaṭ! he says. "Prompt [the Hotṛ] for the fat and omentum of the goat set forth for Prajāpati," he commands. The Maitrāvaruṇa offers the sacrifice with "He who gives life" (ŚB 4.1.8.1), and with "We shall worship him, the giver of strength" (ibid., to the end). At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering. Having proceeded with the omentum, they purify themselves with the three verses beginning "O Waters, you are indeed sources of bliss" (ŚB 4.1.5.1). The treatment of the human head and other animal heads; the *paryagnikaraṇa* of the goat; the *paśu* rite—[the first part being] the sevenfold *iṣṭi* for the *paśupuroḍāśa*. "And twenty-one... He takes [the materials]. Having run to the anthills (*valmīka*) of the ancestors in seven places, he says regarding half of the animal: "Make the head of the animal ready. With both [hands], he replaces the anthill with the head of the animal, saying for the head and the animal: "This I barter for you with these. Thus he speaks.

He scatters seven beans around the human head with the verse, “O leper of this world” (TA 6.5.2). He sings the Yama-gāthā: “Sing for the sake of the earthly one... sing that for which one is obstructed.
He says, “This I purchase from you with these,” as he scatters seven beans around the human head.
He sings the Yama-gāthā: "The seven hotṛs of this one have spread out... and "Seized by the ten girdles in the seat of Vaivasvata, O seven-hotṛ sacrifice...

He scatters this for you... he raises it upward... he performs it. He sings the Yama-gāthā: "In the house of Yama is the sacrifice; therein the pressing-stone, bellowing loudly, dances upright with its stalks."

Regarding this, he says: "Having lifted up the neighbor's jar, having emptied it thoroughly, having removed its meat, having shaken out the brain, and having smeared it with clay, let him set it down.
They do so accordingly.

Then, for her—[they should treat her] as one would a horse, like a bull, like a bull, like a *vṛṣṇi*, like a *vṛṣṇi*, like a goat, like a goat. They should possess their own vital essence and have all their limbs intact; indeed, one should make them appear like testicles.

Having made them out of baked and ground flour, they should cook them just as they cook the *yathāpravartikā* cakes. One should prepare them from clay during a year-long consecration (*saṃvatsaradīkṣā*), or alternatively, from pebbles. Having performed the fire-circumambulation (*paryagnikaraṇa*) together with this animal sacrifice, one should release them; one should certainly not bring the rite to its formal conclusion (*saṃsthāpayet*) with the offering to Prajāpati.

Then they offer these sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*): one on twelve potsherds for Prajāpati, one on twelve potsherds for Vāyu, one on twelve potsherds for Vaiśvānara, a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Kṣatravat, a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Kṣatrabhṛt, a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Brahmaṇvat, and a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Puṣṭimat. Having cooked them, they place them down after spreading a base of butter and pouring butter over them.

They place these animals in front of them: the horse facing west in front; the bull facing east behind; the ram facing north on the south side; and the goat facing south on the north side. In the middle [of the goat] is the head of the one belonging to Prajāpati. [The Adhvaryu says: "Recite for the portion being cut off from the cake for Prajāpati!

He cuts portions both from behind and from the front into the *juhū* ladle, pours clarified butter over them, and anoints them back. He cuts once from the northern half into the *upabhṛt* ladle; he does not pour butter over it, nor does he anoint it back.

In this very manner, having cut off portions from each of these, he cuts off for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering; he does not sprinkle clarified butter over it, nor does he anoint it back. He recites, "Of whom these are the Himālayas... (4.1.8q,1) up to "...we shall worship with greatness" (*mahitvā vidhema*). This is the one who gives the command. He says, "O, cause [the announcement] to be heard! and then issues the command: "Prompt the *maitrāvaruṇa* to announce the cake (*puroḍāśa*) set forth for Prajāpati. The *maitrāvaruṇa* then issues the call.

With the verse, “*yaṃ krandasī* (4.1.8r,1),” he performs the *yajati* offering, concluding with “*avasā tastabhāne vidhema*” (ibid., to the end). When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the oblation and sits down. The Maitrāvaruṇa recites these [verses] as the Hotṛ alone; the Hotṛ performs the *yajati*. [In the case of the animal sacrifice: He says, “Recite for Vāyu,” while spreading [the base of ghee] and cutting [the portions].
He recites, "Fat with food" (TB 2.8.1a), and "They have made [him] an increaser of wealth" (ibid.);
he offers the sacrifice with, "Him for the sake of wealth" (TB 2.8.1b); and at the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the oblation with, "[He] was born as the sole one" (ibid.).

"Recite for Vaiśvānara," he says, while spreading the underlayer and cutting the portions. He recites, "For Vaiśvānara of broad majesty" (RV 3.3.1), and "May your treasures [shine forth] through greatness.
When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he makes the offering.
This is the head of Prajāpati; he sprinkles it with the residue of those [portions].

"Recite for Agni who possesses the *kṣatra*," he says, while spreading the underlayer and cutting the portions. He recites, "With the *kṣatra*, O Agni... (4.1.7e,1), and continues, "...be long-lived, exert yourself, shine here.

(ibid., end)—he offers with, "Right here, O Agni... (4.1.7d,1), and concludes, "...bestow wealth upon us; do not let [the offering] be unestablished. (ibid., end). When the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he makes the offering; he sprinkles the horse with the residue of this [offering].

"Recite for Agni, the sustainer of the kṣatra," he says; while spreading [the base of the ladle] and cutting [the portion], he recites, "Agni, the sustainer of the kṣatra... He recites, "...unwithering, [he has supported] heaven...
He offers with the formula, "...unassailable... He offers the *vaṣaṭ* at the words, "...Jātavedas, our strengthener. He makes the offering when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered.
He bastes the bull with the drippings of this [offering].
He says, "Recite for Agni accompanied by the *brahman*," while spreading [the base of clarified butter] and cutting off [the portions].
He recites, "Thee, O Agni... (4.1.7c,1), and "The Brahmins choose thee... not failing" (ibid., to the end).
He offers with the verse, “O Agni, shine forth” (4.1.7b,1), and [with] “Awaken him, O Mānyu” (ibid., to the end). When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the offering.
He pours the residue over the bull with the formula, “Recite for Agni Puṣṭimat,” while spreading [the butter] underneath and cutting [the portions].

Having cut off portions here for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he cuts off twice and pours clarified butter over them twice. He does not anoint them back. He recites: “On the navel of the earth” (VS 4.1.10d), and “Kindling the fire... the victorious one” (ibid.). He performs the sacrifice with the verse: “Day after day” (VS 11.75), and “Bringing [the oblation] without ceasing... may we not come to harm” (ibid.). When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he offers the oblation.
Having set down [the butter], he sprinkles [the oblation] with its residue;
he says, "Recite for Agni," while pouring together [the butter] for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering of the sacrificial cakes;
he recites, "When the waters... (*TS* 4.1.8.1), ending with "...thereby let us worship the gods" (*ibid.*); this [recitation] includes the formal command (*praiṣa*).

Saying "O, announce! (*o śrāvaya*), he issues the command: "Recite the invitatory verse for Agni" (*agnaye 'nubrūhi*). The Maitrāvaruṇa priest recites the offering verse beginning with "He who indeed [the waters]" (*yaś cid āpaḥ*) and ending with "with greatness we shall worship" (*mahinā vidhema*). When the *vaṣaṭ* call is uttered, he makes the oblation.
Having stepped across and placed the two offering-spoons in their proper places, and having divided the portions of the sacrificial food, he places the *iḍā* portion before the Hotṛ.

When the *iḍā* has been invoked, he places [the portions] for the *agnīdh*. They consume [the portions], they purify themselves, and the rite is completed; from this point on, it is the sacrifice of the oblation itself. Standing up, the Adhvaryu says, "Recite the invitatory prayer for the goat-oblation to Prajāpati," while the Pratiprasthātṛ takes the fat-offering (*vasāhoma*).

He recites, “By whom the sky, O fierce one... (4.1.8s,1), and concludes with, “...and the earth, may we worship them firmly” (ibid., end). This is the one who issues the command; he says, “O, cause it to be heard!
(M247), and then the Maitrāvaruṇa priest issues the direction: “For Prajāpati, of the goat... [of the] fat... standing for the oblation, give the command! (8). Thus he commands.
"He knows it"—thus he sacrifices; "the son [sacrifices] for the father who has become [the deity]" (TB 3.5.7.2)—thus he offers when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered;
the two *triṣṭubh* verses are the *saṃyājyās*. This is the other deliberation regarding the animal sacrifice—now, there are these other eight *ṛc*s.

Of these, there is one *āghāra* libation for the omentum, two for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), and two for the oblations (*havis*). He omits two of these; of these, he offers one as the *iḍā*. "O Agni, bestow..."—with this very verse, the ritual action for the sacrificial cakes is accomplished. The rite concludes with the oblation for Prajāpati. The animal sacrifice for Prajāpati is completed.
"Prakāravo mananā-ghṛtācī"— thus are established the *saṃbhāras* (preparatory materials) for the *dīkṣaṇīyā* of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice:
the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering and the production of the fire for the *ukhya* hearth.

[The *dīkṣaṇīyeṣṭi*: Now, the other two items are the two fire-pan lids (*ukhā*), the *muñja* grass, the *kramuka* wood, the stool (*āsandī*), the sling (*śikya*), the gold plate (*rukma*), the cord (*pāśa*), and two pieces of black antelope skin for trimming; one of these has a gold plate with twenty-one knobs fastened to it. There are three fans (*dhavitra*), two leaf-sprigs (*parṇavakala*), twelve fuel-sticks—five of *vaikaṅkata*, one of *śamī*, five of *udumbara*, one of *aśvattha*, one of *vaikaṅkata*, one of *śamī*, and two of *udumbara*.

Having arranged the sacrificial implements and having carried forward the water, he offers the *dīkṣaṇīyā* oblation dedicated to Agni and Viṣṇu on eleven potsherds, as well as an oblation to Vaiśvānara on twelve potsherds and a pap (*caru*) to Āditya. Once these have been poured out, he recites the *prāṇagrahas* and the *pṛśni* verses.

Having released his speech at the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*), he offers the *saptahotṛ* formula with four spoonfuls into the *āhavanīya* fire for the twelve seasons, saying: "To Madhu, svāhā! To Mādhava, svāhā!"—and so forth.

The thirty-three bodies of sacrifice—referring to the verses beginning with “Prajāpati, blind with his mind, sought” (4.4.9)—are recited while the oblations are being cooked; he performs the *stambayajus* rite, encloses the altar (*vedi*), and mutters the *karaṇa* formula.
Thus the ritual action of what has been studied from the *yajus* formulas is successfully accomplished.
With the *sruva* ladle, he offers the sacrificial formulas (*yajūṃṣi*) of the recited portion: “To Ākūti, to Prayuj, to Agni, svāhā! Having offered with the *sruva* ladle, saying:

“From the firm one, for wisdom—with the oblation may he increase; svāhā! To Ākūti, to Agni Prayuj, svāhā! To the mind, to Agni Vaiśvānara, svāhā! (4.1.9a)—he causes the *dhruvā* vessel to swell with the *juhū* ladle, saying: “For prosperity, svāhā! (4.1.9b).
Then, silently pouring out the *praṇītā* water within the altar, he spreads the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) within the altar.
He creeps forward in a well-established manner; he succeeds because of the sprinkling of the fingers,
for the finger itself is not sprinkled.
Then, with the two verses beginning, “Do not tremble, do not be harmed” (4.1.9c, 1), he places the fire-pan (*ukhā*) upon the embers of the Āhavanīya fire.

Into it, he places *muñja* grass, horse-hair, cow-dung, *bṛnbā* plants, last year’s straw, and pieces of wood. He stands over it with the verse, “Be firm, be strong; in this one... (4.1.9d, variant), and with “O Mitra, heat this pan” (4.1.9e, 1). Then they fan it with the verse, “This one... against the attack” (ibid., to the end and *f*).
They desire to produce fire either in the east or in the north, [reciting] "O wood-eater, whose libation is clarified butter" (4.1.9g).
Once it has been produced, he offers a *krumuka* stick mixed with clarified butter with a *sruva*-ladle, [reciting] "The ancient, wonderful one, *svāhā*" (from the same passage, ending with *svāhā*).

Then, [reciting] "From the highest enclosure" (4.1.9h), he places a piece of *vaikaṅkata* wood [on the fire], [reciting] "Downward from the lower one, *svāhā*" (from the same passage, ending with *svāhā*).
With the verse, “From the highest distance” (4.1.9i,1), he offers an oblation made of *śamī* wood. With the verse, “The ruddy-horse one, crossing over the adversaries, svāhā!
(ibid., end), he performs the *Viṣṇukrama* steps while the *ukhyāgni* fire is present.

With the three verses beginning, “Sit down in the lap of this mother” (4.1.9k,1), and ending with “O Agni, all things... sit here in your own womb” (ibid., end and verses l–m), he worships the fire once it has been produced.

With the verse, “Whatever [fires], O Agni... (4.1.10a), he places five [fire-sticks] of *udumbara* wood; with “I place [thee] in thy mouth, svāhā! (ibid., end of a–e, with *svāhā*), [he places] those of *aśvattha* wood; with “The burglars with thy two tusks... (4.1.10f, with *svāhā*), [he places] those of *vaikaṅkata* wood; and with “Those who among men are burglars... (4.1.10g, with *svāhā*), [he places those of *vaikaṅkata* wood]. With “The thieves and robbers... crush them, svāhā! (ibid., end of f, with *svāhā*), [he places those of *aśvattha* wood].
With the mantra, “He who acts with hostility toward us” (4.1.10h,1), he offers a twig of *śamī* wood; with “And him who [acts so], reduce him to ashes, svāhā!

(at the end of the same, with *svāhā*), and with “May my sacred word (*brahman*) be sharpened” (4.1.10i,1), he causes the sacrificer to recite over the final *audumbara* twig: “Sharpened for me—svāhā! (at the end of the same, with *svāhā*).

At this time, to the south of the *āhavanīya* fire, an *audumbara* stool is prepared. Then, with the verse, "As a mother her son, may the earth bear the one who is worthy of the soil" (*ŚB* 4.2.5e,1), he takes hold of the *ukhā* pot with two *parṇa*-leaves. With the formula, "May the *ukhā* support Agni in his own womb; may Prajāpati Viśvakarman join it together with all the gods," he places the clay and other materials upon the twelve-spoked wooden frame.

While seated, he puts on the gold plate with the verse, “The shining gold plate” (4.1.10 l, 1), ending with “the wide earth, the one of good seed” (ibid.). With the verse, “All forms” (4.1.10 m, 1), ending with “the seer shines forth from the east” (ibid.), he [addresses] Agni.
With the verse, “Night and Dawn” (4.1.10 n, 1), ending with “the two of different forms, united in mind, the giver of wealth” (ibid.), he cuts out the black antelope skin.

He worships with the words, “Thou art the fair-winged Garuḍa” (4.1.10o,1). “The Trivṛt is thy head, the Gāyatra is thy eye... the Yajus-mantras are thy name” (ibid., to the end)—“Thou art the fair-winged Garuḍa; go to heaven, fly to the light” (4.1.10p)—with these words he rises.

Having performed the Viṣṇu-strides with the formula, "Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu" (4.2.1a1), he steps across this fire with the mantra, "O slayer of the adversary, ascend the Gāyatrī metre; stride along the quarters; deprived of his share is he whom we hate" (4.2.1a1 to the end).
He recites one verse, "He has roared" (4.2.1b,1), ending with "Agni thunders within" (ibid., to the end).
He turns back with the four verses beginning, "O Agni, thou who turnest toward us" (4.2.1c,1), [ending with] "Turn toward us... (to the end).

"From all sides... (ibid. c to the end, and up to f)—with the verse beginning "O Varuṇa, loosen the highest bond from us" (4.2.1g,1), he releases one [bond]; with the verse beginning "May we be for the release of the lowest... (ibid. to the end?)—[he releases another] with "Bring thee hither" (4.2.1h,1); ... with "Thou hast become within... all... (4.2.1h to the end, and i).
With the four verses beginning, “Sit down in the lap of this mother” (4.2.1k,1), he worships him as he lies there. With the Vātsapra hymn, beginning with “O Agni, all [beings]...
the great Truth” (4.2.1k to the end-n) and “Agni was first born from heaven” (4.2.2a,1), he worships him, reciting this entire section without interruption.

"Madhuś ca Mādhavaś ca"—with these two seasons... [the breaths] indeed... svāhā; "yena devāḥ svasti svāhā"; "trīṇy āyūṃṣi śaṃ yo svāhā"—with these he sprinkles his fingers; thus the rite succeeds when they bring him the vow-food.

"O Lord of Food, give us food"—with these words, he places two fuel-sticks (*samidh*) as attendants to the vow (*vratānucaryau*). [He continues: "To the one free from disease—for the two-footed and the four-footed, *svāhā*. ... "O sacrificer, well-being, *svāhā*! ... These two fuel-sticks as attendants to the vow are placed at the beginning of the vow; whenever the vow is handed over, they remain there.
In the morning, having released his speech by means of the sun, while sitting, he fastens on the gold plate (*rukma*) with the verse: "The shining gold plate... (4.1.10).

With the verse, "All forms" (4.1.10m,1), he [addresses] Agni; with "Night and Dawn" (4.1.10n,1), he [addresses] the one who has trimmed the black antelope skin; with "You are the fair-winged Garuḍa" (4.1.10o,1), he worships [the skin];

with "You are the fair-winged Garuḍa, go to heaven, fly to the light" (4.1.10p), he rises. He strides the Viṣṇu-strides with "Of Viṣṇu... [etc.]. They do not indeed remove this fire from him. He recites only the single verse, "He cried out" (4.2.1b,1).
He turns around with the four verses beginning, "O Agni, you who turn toward us" (4.2.1c–f);
he releases [the horse] with the single verse, "Loosen the highest bond from us, O Varuṇa" (4.2.1g); and he brings it back with the two verses, "I have brought you hither" (4.2.1h–i).
He worships the seated [Agni] with the four verses beginning, “Sit down, O Haṃsa, dwelling in purity” (RV 4.40.5);

with the six [verses] beginning, “Madhu and Mādhava” (RV 1.164.1–6), he worships day after day; and with the verses, “By which the gods [attained immortality],” and “Three lifespans” (RV 3.2.11f), he places these fuel-sticks on the fire. He performs the Viṣṇu-strides during the day.
That evening, every night, he places these same fuel-sticks on the fire with the verses, “By which the gods [attained immortality],” and “Three lifespans.”
In this very manner, he proceeds by means of these two yogas in turn. Having performed the Viṣṇu-strides, they dwell there.
In the morning, having released his speech with the sun, he worships with the Vātsapra hymn using this Anuvāka, "From heaven Agni was first born," without interruption.
With the six [verses], beginning with "iṣaś corjaś ca" (4.4.11d,1?), he worships the subsequent seasons day after day;

with the verses "yena devās" (5.7.2.c,1) and "trīṇy āyūṃṣi" (3.2.11f,1), he places these kindling-sticks (samidh) on the fire. On that day, at nightfall, he places these kindling-sticks with the verses "yena devās" and "trīṇy āyūṃṣi" every single night.

In this very manner, he proceeds by means of these two yogas alternately: the Viṣṇukrama [sacrifice] on the first day and the Vātsapra on the subsequent day. If the first day is indeed the Viṣṇukrama and the subsequent day the Vātsapra, and if the yoga should approach the consecrated one at the time of the Viṣṇukramas, he should perform the yoga after having stepped forward with those strides.
<14> The preparation of the Āhavanīya hearth; the preparation of the Uttaravedi.
If he performs the worship after concluding the Vātsapra rite, having heated the sacrificial vessels and bound the calves together—at the conclusion of the ritual application (yoga)—[K1,55a7].

With the verse, "Upward indeed you, O All-Gods" (4.2.3b,1), he lifts the fire; with "O Agni, may they bring wealth" (ibid., end), he places the water-jar (kavandha) down; and with the four verses beginning "Sit thou down, the swan dwelling in purity" (4.2.1k,1 & n,1), he pays reverence to the fire that has been set down.
"O Agni, come forth as one possessing light"—with this single verse he proceeds. "With auspicious bodies, [protect] the offspring"—[this is the end of the citation].

"Honor the fire with fuel"—with this verse, once the fire has settled, he places a fuel-stick (*samidh*) that has been sprinkled with clarified butter (*ghṛta*). "Awaken [the gods] with clarified butter, offer the oblation, *svāhā*"—with this [verse, including *svāhā* at the end].
"This Agni of the Bharata has become widely renowned"—with this [verse], for a Kṣatriya. "He who is auspicious like... [the rest of the verse follows].

With the words, “Svāhā” (at the end of the same passage, including “svāhā”), [he performs the rites for] the piling of the Gārhapatya fire on the next day, the mixing of the ashes on the following day, and the purchase of the King [Soma] on the next day.

Then, with the three verses beginning, “O divine waters, receive these ashes” (4.2.3f,1), he causes the ashes to enter the water in a vessel made of Udumbara wood, using the verses, “Make a pleasant seat... you are the embryo of the waters” (4.2.3f,2–h).
With the two verses, "Having propitiated the womb with ashes" (4.2.3i,1–k), he touches the primary fire; with the verse, "The waters and the earth, O Agni, most auspicious...
(4.2.3i,2–k), and with the two verses, "Return again with strength" (4.2.3l,1–m), he strokes himself. With the verse, "Again, O Agni, from all sides...

(4.2.3l,2–m), and with the single verse, "May the Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus kindle thee again" (4.2.3n,1), he kindles the *ukhya* fire; and with the verse, "Again, may the Brahmins... the desires of the sacrificer" (ibid. o, to the end).
He worships with the verse, “O youngest one, understand this our speech” (4.2.3o,1), ending with “of the most generous one... [ward off] hostilities” (ibid.).
They dig a trench for the Gārhapatya altar’s mound, measuring as much as a chariot wheel, and having dug it, they fill it in with pebbles.
Having gone out and measured the great altar (mahāvedi), at the time for the northern altar (uttaravedi), he measures the gold.
Having measured it, they dig around it. They enclose the trench with pebbles (śarkarā). Having enclosed it with pebbles, they dwell [therein].
[This concludes] the first layer of the Āhavanīya fire-altar.

The materials for the *gārhapatya* hearth: cf. Caland, *Vierte M.* No. 114, p. 235; for the *gārhapatyaciti*, cf. Caland, op. cit., No. 115, pp. 235–6. Cf. *Akh.* <15>, 610–611 (C) No. 114–115, pp. 235–6.

Having released his speech at dawn with the *āditya* [offering], if it is the time for the *viṣṇukrama* steps, or if it is the time for the *vātsapra* [hymn], he performs only the *viṣṇukrama* steps. [K4,55a11]
He worships with the *vātsapra* hymns; he worships with both [sets] day after day.
He places these kindling-sticks (*samidh*) upon the fire with the verses beginning, "With which the gods... (5.7.2c), "The three lifespans... (3.2.11f), and "Worship Agni with fuel" (TS 4.2.3d).
They pour this fire together into a vessel, sprinkle it, and having taken the fire into himself, he mutters the *svayañcit* formula.
With the formula, “Thou art power” (KS 39.5; cf. ĀpŚS 16.29.2), he puts on a sandal made of black antelope skin.

With the formula, “May Vāc place thee upon the ocean” (KS 38.13:116.1–3; cf. ĀpŚS 19.11.11), he pours out a vessel of water in the middle of the Gārhapatya altar-mound and places [the sandal] down with the formula, “Granting good offspring, granting abundance of wealth for me, O vigorous one; by that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras” (KS 38.13:116.1–3).

With the formula, "Sit thou firm," he places that [brick] upon it: "Thou art the hairy brick, the luminous; thee I place for this world, for yonder world, for attainment, for pervasion, for completion, for the fulfillment of desire, for the heavenly world. Do thou recognize the heavenly world! May Prajāpati settle thee on the back of the earth; by that deity, sit thou firm like Aṅgiras. (cf. KS 38.13:116.2-3)

With the words, “Thou art the ash of Agni” (4.2.4b1), he scatters the ash; with “Thou art the soil of Agni” (ibid. b2), the soil; with “Thou art auspicious knowledge, the sustainer of desires” (4.2.4c1), the sand; and with “May thy sustaining of desires be in me,” the saline earth (*ūṣān*). With the verse, “That which is your dear body” (4.2.4d), he mixes them together, saying, “May it be dear to me.
Thus he recites the *hotṛ*-formulas over these ritual materials.

With the formula, “O you who abide in the mind, well-known” (TS 4.2.7 l,1), he lays down the limited [sand]; with the formula, “Resting upright, lend support to the sacrificer; by that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras” (*ibid.*, at the end), he repeats this for each layer; with the formula, “Swell up; let it come together unto thee” (TS 4.2.7 m,1), he spreads out the Soma-related sand; and with the formula, “From all sides, O you who are joined” (*ibid.*, at the end), he pours out the sand with the formula, “May your milks be auspicious” (TS 4.2.7 n,1). . . . Thus he concludes.

He causes four bricks facing eastward to be laid out for the middle Gārhapatya altar. He makes [the sacrificer] recite the *haṃsapātinī* verses while they are being placed facing northward: with the hymn of Viśvāmitra, "This is that Agni" (4.2.4e); with "In whom, O Indra, Soma... O Jātavedas" [end of verse]; with "By that deity... O Agni, the flood from heaven, the waters... (4.2.4f); with "By that deity"; with "O Agni, what of thine in heaven... O thou who beholdest men" (4.2.4g); with "By that deity"; and with "The Agnis of the soil... the great ones" (4.2.4h).

With the formula, "By that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras" (4.2.4e–h)—the *tayā devatayā* mantra being added to each—one places two bricks facing each other in the east with the formulas, "O Agni, the *iḍā*" (4.2.4i,1) and "The one of many wondrous deeds, the winner of cattle... (to the end of the same). With "By that deity," and with the formula for the other brick, "This is your seasonal womb" (4.2.4k,1), ending with "...from which wealth [flows]" (to the end of the same), followed by "By that deity... sit."

With the formula, “*cid asi*” (4.2.4l,1?), he places two bricks facing each other behind [the altar]; with “*tayā devatayā, paricid asi*” (4.2.4m,1), he places the others; and with “*tayā deva... sīda*” (ibid., to the end), he extends thirteen *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks.
This concludes the second section on the *gārhapatya* piling.

Facing them with the formula, “Fill the world” (TS 4.2.4n,1), he places the first one by spreading them out: “Fill the gap; sit down, you who are auspicious; may Indra, Agni, and Bṛhaspati seat you in this womb” (ibid., to the end); “With that deity, those [bricks] of his yield milk” (TS 4.2.4o,1). With the verse, “The dappled ones mix the Soma from heaven” (ibid., to the end), and with the formula, “With that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras” (ibid., to the end, and the *tayā devatā* mantra)—[K4,55b5].
In this very manner, he lays down these [bricks] accompanied by their respective formulas one by one.

He touches them with the *Citi-kḷpti* formula: "The piled and the unpiled" (5.5.4.4). Then, [he recites]: "Like a piler, the wise one, protect the back... sit with her" (at the end of the same passage), and the *Tayādevata* mantra. Then, with the verse "Heaven-backed" (1.5.11d,1; TB 3.11.6.4,1), he lays down the layer of loose earth (*purīṣa*), saying: "Agni, heaven-backed, may he protect... night... sit with her, O deity" (at the end of the same passage, and the *Tayādevata* mantra).
He touches [the altar] with the words, “consciousness and unconsciousness” (5.5.4.4), and [concludes] with “sit down by means of that” (Taittirīya Saṃhitā mantra).
Regarding this, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage stating, “One should pile [the altar] with five layers, three layers, or one layer.

If one were to act in accordance with that, he would not employ this Vaiśvāmitra hymn; rather, he should lay down twenty-one *lokapṛṇā* bricks and a layer of loose earth (*purīṣa*). Twenty-one *lokapṛṇā* bricks and a layer of loose earth are established right here.

With the four verses beginning, "Right here let there be peace" (4.2.5a–d), while looking elsewhere as he pours together [the contents], he says: "May you two, being well-disposed, radiant, and of kindly mind, agree; may you both be auspicious unto us today.

(4.2.5a–d) He pours into the cauldron (*ukhā*) a drop of clarified butter, a drop of curds, and a drop of honey. He fills it with sand. In this same way he pours [the contents] into the upper one, and in this same way he prepares the other cauldron.

Then, with the two leaf-splinters, he encloses the fire-pan (*ukhā*) with the verse, “Like a mother her son, the earth [holds] the one worthy of the soil” (4.2.5e,1); and with the verse, “Agni has been brought to his own womb; may Viśvakarman release him” (ibid., to the end), they fasten the sling upon the wooden frames (*khārī*).

They release the gold from the noose. Three black Nairṛta bricks are baked with chaff. To the south, west, and toward the self-made pit, they tether the enemy. Or, having gone to a fissure or a water-vessel, they cross over the Nairṛta bricks with the verse, “That which is beyond this dust” (TS 4.2.5f,1). Having gone there, he takes up the sling-noose with the formula, “The bright light, O Vaiśvānara, the resplendent... (*ibid.*, ending with *svāhā* instead of *dyumat* in the TS).

With the mantra, "Homage to thee, O Nirṛti" (TS 4.2.5g,1; in the TS version without "tan"), he places a tuft of wool with its tip turned away [from him] upon a self-made depression or a cleft, saying, "Make this one ascend the iron [fetter]" (ibid., omitting *viśvarūpe* as found in the TS).

Then, with the mantra, "What thou, O Goddess Nirṛti, hast bound" (TS 4.2.5h,1), he lays down the Nairṛta bricks upon that [depression], facing away and not touching one another. He does not [thereby] make [the victim] subject to the deity. With the mantra, "The bond from the neck... homage be to thee, O Goddess Nirṛti" (TS 4.2.5h to the end, k).

He pours down the earth; he throws down the cord of the gold plate. They worship with the verse: "As great as heaven and earth are in their greatness" (3.2.6b), and: "And as far as the seven rivers have spread out, so far does the goddess Nirṛti, who possesses all forms, know of every being that is born. O goddess, I would fain avoid the great Nirṛti. Having sprinkled water around, they return without looking back.

Having entered the hall and cleansed themselves, they worship the Āhavanīya fire and the Gārhapatya altar with the verse, “The assembler of riches, the dwelling place... (TS 4.2.5m,1), and then with the verse, “He beholds all forms on the paths... (ibid., to the end). Then, having arranged the sacrificial implements and led forward the waters, he offers the Prāyaṇīya oblation; having performed the Prāyaṇīya, he purchases the King Soma. ... Having purchased [the King], he prepares the Ātithya offering for him.
Having performed the *ātithyeṣṭi*, he proceeds with the *pravargya* and the *upasad* rites.
[Now follows] the preparation of the fire-altar site (*agnikṣetra*).

Now he describes this ritual action: the *stambayajus* and the enclosing of the altar (*vedi*), the performance of the rite, the taking of the fire, the self-piling (*svayañciti*), the shoe, the plow, the oxen, the mixing, the yoking, the plowing, the brick, the oblation, the water-vessel, all the herbs, the water-vessel, the high altar (*uttaravedi*), the boundaries of the quarters, the eight thunderbolt-bearers, the pouring of sand, the measured [sand], and the arrangement of the sand.

This is his duty: he carries away the *stambayajus*, encloses the altar (*vedi*), mutters the *karaṇa* formula, takes the fire within himself, and mutters the *svayaṃcit* formula. He puts on a black leather sandal with the words, "Thou art power. With two verses, "Bind the straps together," he joins the plow and the plowshare. [He proceeds] with the words, "O plow, thou art the inexhaustible one. (TS 4.2.5.n–o)

With two verses, "The ploughmen yoke the ploughs" (4.2.5p,1) and "The seers [yoked] the yokes... (ibid. p–q), he joins [the ploughs]. With two verses, "...the plough with iron-tipped share" (4.2.5r,1) and "...[bestow] upon us... (ibid. r–s), he ploughs. He ploughs three furrows toward the east with the verse, "...grant us prosperity... (4.2.5r to the end and s).

In the same way, three [furrows] run northward along the two wings; in the same way, from the northern hip... [they run] toward the northern shoulder; from the southern hip, they turn back toward the south.

With the words, "Release them, the paths leading to the gods that lead to prosperity," he releases them to the north behind the fire with the mantra, "We have crossed to the further shore of this darkness; we have reached the light. With the words, "O yielder of desires, milk out our desire," he consecrates the heads of the furrows. With the words, "For Mitra, for Varuṇa... for all creatures," [he concludes].

"Anointed with ghee and honey"—with this, at the meeting point of the furrows (*sītā-samara*), he places gold upon it and offers an oblation of four spoonfuls: "With all the gods—with milk—turn hither, svāhā! (*ibid.*, ending with *svāhā*).

With the formula, "May Vāc place thee upon the ocean," (*KS* 38.13:116.1–3), he pours out a vessel of water in the middle of the meeting point of the furrows and deposits [the gold], saying: "Bestowing good offspring—for the sake of vigor—sit down with her. (*ibid.*, ending as above).

Upon that [altar], he places this [brick]—the *śalila*-brick, which is luminous—with the formula: "Thee, who art luminous, I place for that world and for this world, for attainment, for pervasion, for completion, for desire, for the heavenly world. Do thou recognize the heavenly world! May Prajāpati settle thee on the back of heaven; sit down with her. (cf.
KS 38.13:116.2–3) [Then follow] the *dharma*-bricks, etc., the sprinkling of the fire (*agnyavokṣaṇa*), and the shaving (*vapana*). (K1,56a5–11; K4,56a6–11; M256–7)
One should prepare three *mahāvīra* vessels for the piling of the fire-altar.

Whichever of those [bricks] he intends to place down first, with that he should proceed. Having filled it with curds, he places the *gharma*-brick—touching neither [other bricks] nor the location for the *svayamātṛṇṇā*—to the north-east, with the mantra: "In me is that great power (*indriya*)... (*mayi tyad indriyaṃ mahat*, TB 3.7.9.4f,1; TA 4.21.1,1; cf. Dumont, TB p. 330 n. 30). Then: "In me is skill... O *gharma*, may the pain of women shine forth... may we obtain the milk-yielding... sit with her" (*mayi dakṣo... gharma strīśug virocata... doham aśīmahi, tayā... sīda*; TB 3.7.9f,2; TA 4.21.1,2 & *tayā devatā*).
With the *tāyā devatā* formula, "With that [brick], sit down," he places the *daśahotṛ* at the time of the naturally perforated brick (*svayamātṛṇṇā*).

With the formula, "Puṣṭi is the metre," he places a clump of *darbha* grass, not touching [the brick], to the north-east of the location of the naturally perforated brick, with the *tāyā devatā* formula, "With that [clump], sit down."

With five [verses], he makes offerings with the fivefold-drawn [ghee], [reciting]: "In harmony with the year, with the waters, svāhā! (5.6.4.1, [1]); "In harmony with the dawn, with the ruddy ones, svāhā! In harmony with Sūrya, with Etaśa, svāhā! In harmony with the Aśvins, with their wondrous deeds, svāhā! In harmony with Agni Vaiśvānara, with the *iḍā*-invocations and with ghee, svāhā! (ibid. [2]–[5]).

He mixes all the herbs with curds while reciting, “Sing forth to Parjanya” (*TB* 2.4.5.5; *TA* 1.29). Before the mixture of all the herbs, he sprinkles the fire with water from a water-pot while reciting, “May he desire fodder for the son of Heaven” (*TB* 2.4.5.5;

*TA* 1.29). With the three verses beginning, “The herbs that have been born” (4.2.6a–c), he sows three furrows facing eastward, using the verses ending with, “For the gods... the deliverers” (4.2.6a to the end-c).

With the three verses beginning, “O plants, mothers” (4.2.6d–f), he follows the two wings toward the north; with the verse, “I address you, O goddesses, so that you may seize the misdeeds” (4.2.6d to the end), and with the three verses beginning, “When the plants come together” (4.2.6g–i), he [covers] from the northern hip toward the southern shoulder, ending with, “The king [has protected us]; protect our speech” (4.2.6g to the end).
With the three verses beginning, “O *ucchusmā*, [thou art] of the plants” (4.2.6k–m), he [addresses] from the southern hip toward the northern shoulder;

then with the two verses beginning, “O *yakṣma*, fly away like a bird to its nest” (4.2.6n–o), he causes the ends [of the body] to be extended along [the limbs], ending with, “[with] the *śyena* and the *kikidīvi*, for the sake of safety” (4.2.6n to the end).

With the two verses beginning, "Those which bear fruit, those which are fruitless" (4.2.6p, 1), he purifies himself; [the second verse] ending with, "And those that are flowerless—[I purify you] for the sake of life" (4.2.6p to the end, q).

With the verse, “O you who speak clearly, may your union...,” he sprinkles the fire from above with water containing all herbs. Then, with the mantra, “Praise Parjanya with songs; let the bellowing bull, the swift bestower of moisture, pour his seed into the plants as a germ,” he pours out the earth for the *uttaravedi* according to the procedure for the *uttaravedi*.

He throws clods of earth from the various directions, saying, "Do not harm us. From the east, he brings a clod, placing it upon a stone with the formula: "He who is the progenitor of the earth—to him we shall offer oblation. (Concluding with *TS* 4.2.7a).

Having ascended from the west, he places the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick at the eastern end with the *tayā devatā* formula: "By that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras" (*tayā devatayāṅgirasvad dhruvā sīda*). With the formula "Turn toward us, O Earth" (*abhyāvartasva pṛthivī*), he places it to the south. Having ascended again from the west, he places the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick at the southern end with the *tayā devatā* formula: "By that deity, sit firm. With the formula "O Agni, that which is thy bright... (*agne yat te śukram*) at the western end, he continues: "...that which is radiant, that which is pure, that which is worthy of sacrifice—we bring it" (to the end of the verse).

Having mounted [the cart] again with another [man], he himself places the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick at the proper time with the *tayādevata* formula, "With her sit thou," and [with the formula] "Food and strength I take from here" (TS 4.2.7d). If there should be something belonging to that direction, he should bring a clod of earth from there and place it to the north with the formula, "From the abode of Ṛta... [remove] my disease" (ibid.).
Having mounted [the cart] from the north side at a later time, he himself places the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick with the *tayā devatā* formula: "By that deity... sit down.

Then he places the *vajriṇī* bricks. Prior to this, four stones have been prepared for him. Standing to the east of the fire, facing eastward, he throws one outside the altar with the verse, "He sat down, the slayer of Vṛtra," and then another with, "The protector of our bodies, the far-seeing one."
Where the arrow strikes, from there he takes the dust and places that stone down with the formula: "May he who seeks to harm us from the east strike this stone" (ŚB 6.7.2.8).
Having climbed up from the west, he places it to the east of the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick with the formula: "By that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm! (TS 4.2.4.1).
Standing to the south of the fire, he places it to the south with the formula: "Of Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra... (TS 5.7.3a2,1; cf. TB 1.7.9).
He throws [the brick] outside the altar with the formula, “*tanūpā-*”;

he places it down with the formula, “*yo no dakṣiṇato ’ghāyur abhidāsati etaṃ saḥ*. Having climbed up by that very path, he places it to the south of the *svayamātṛṇṇā* with the *tayādevata* formula, “*tayā sīda*,” and with the formula, “*indrasya rtraghna*,” while standing behind the fire and facing westward, he throws [the brick] onto the *barhis* and places it down.

"He who, being malicious, shall attack us from behind—let him strike this stone! Having climbed up, he places another *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick at its time with the *tayādevata* formula, "Sit down with that," and with the mantra, "Thou art Indra’s thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra" (5.7.3a4,1; cf. TB 1.7.9), standing to the north of the fire and facing northward, he hurls it outside the altar, saying, "He who, being malicious, shall attack us from the north—let him strike this stone! (ibid. 3).
Having climbed up again from the north, he himself places the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick with the *tayā devatā* formula: “With that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras.
With the six verses beginning, “O Agni, your fame and vigor” (4.2.7e–k), he scatters sand.

He places the measured bricks with the formula, “You are piled, you are piled around” (= 4.2.7 l, 1). He places them with the formula, “Supporting yourselves upright, support the sacrificer; with that deity... sit” (4.2.7 l to the end).

With the verse, “May you swell; may [the waters] come together unto you” (TS 4.2.7m), he spreads out the Soma-sand (*saumyās sikatāḥ*). With the verse, “From all sides, O you who are well-united” (ibid.), and with the verse, “Peaceful be your milks” (TS 4.2.7n), he does so for a *rājanya*.
This is the great altar-pile (*mahāciti*), the collection of materials (*saṃbhāra*). These are the preliminary rites.
To the east of the hall, they pile up this great altar on a skin with the hair facing upward.

Its enumeration consists of: the horse; the materials for the high altar (*uttaravedi*); the sprinkling waters; the taking of the fire; the self-piling (*svayañciti*); the shoe; the two steps; the brick for the ascent; the sprinkling with clarified butter (*vyāghāra*); the footprint of the horse; another portion; the cups (*graha*); the division; the jar-bricks (*kumbheṣṭakā*); the oblation for Bṛhaspati; thirteen chips of gold; a lotus leaf; a golden plate; a human figure; two ladles full of clarified butter; and one made of *kārṣmarya* wood.

An *udumbara* vessel filled with curds; the *sarpa-yajus* bricks; the *svayamātṛṇṇā*; the gold brick (*hiraṇyeṣṭakā*); the circle brick (*maṇḍaleṣṭakā*); two *dūrvā* bricks; two earthen cooking pots (*sthālī*); those which are silver; the *vāmabhṛt*; the *virāj*; the *retassik*; the *viśvajyotis*; the *tryālikhitā*; two seasonal (*ṛtavyā*) bricks; eight *avakā* plants; one *saṃyānī*; nine *sayuṅ* bricks; the head-bricks; the tortoise; curds mixed with honey; the mortar and pestle; rice and barley; and two fire-pannels (*ukhā*).

There are five animal heads, two pieces of gold, seven others, five others, fifteen *apasyā* bricks, five *chandasyā* bricks, fifty *prāṇabhṛt* bricks, fifty *apānabhṛt* bricks, twelve wombs, the limbs of Agni, the one belonging to Prajāpati, and the bull; the *sāmaciti*, the *sāman* verses, the nine *lokaṃpṛṇā* bricks, and the single *lokaṃpṛṇā* brick; the outer layer, the joint, the touching, the *gāyatrī* verse, the oblation of the Hotṛ, the descent, and the worship—this constitutes its ritual performance.
When this has been thus agreed upon, the *adhvaryu* enters, takes four portions of clarified butter, and offers it into the *āhavanīya* fire with the verse:
"O mortals, make Agni your god, most skilled in sacrifice, the messenger at the rite, who is established among men, the observer of Truth, the head that burns, the purifier" (KS 35.1:51.5–6).
He then takes another four portions.

He offers that with the verse: “And you go, O Savitṛ, to the three luminous realms of heaven; you traverse the night on both sides; you unite with the rays of the sun; and you become Mitra, O God, by your ordinances—svāhā! (ṚV 5.81.4).
Having taken up the sprinkling waters, he steps out with the formula:

“I sprinkle you, the fires, as acceptable to the fires. He then sprinkles the piled altar with the formula: “I sprinkle you, the fires, as acceptable to the fires. (BŚS 10.27:269-10). He sprinkles the altar that has been constructed.

"Recite for Agni as the fires are being led forth," he says. Having set out with the horse foremost and having run past, he sprinkles the northern navel [of the altar] with the mantra: "May Indra’s roar protect you from the east along with the Vasus" (TS 1.2.12.2i).
Whatever remains of the *prokṣaṇī* waters, he pours out to the south of the *mahāvedi*, outside the measured area, along the track of the wooden sword (*sphya*).
While doing so, the sacrificer meditates upon whomsoever he hates.
Having touched water, he then fastens the fire within himself.

With the verse, “Indraṃ viśvā avīvṛdhan” (4.6.4m,1; cf. 5.4.6.5), he lays down the *ākramaṇa* brick with the formula: “This very earth, as wide as the ocean... O lord of the sattra, sit upon her. (K4,56b12–K4,57b12)

With the mantra, “This is the gathering place of the waters” (4.6.1 l,1), he ascends by means of the mounting-wood. [He recites: “The dwelling-place of the ocean—be auspicious” (ibid., end); “Homage to your heat—be auspicious” (M260); “May speech be in my mouth” (4.6.1m; 5.5.9g[1]); “Strength in my thighs; may all my limbs be uninjured; may my body be with my self; homage be to you; do not harm me” (5.5.9g, end). “That I implore of you, praising you with sacred knowledge; that he desires... (10) ...he causes him to cross over by means of the left eye.

Having laid around the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) made of *pautudrava* wood and having piled up the ritual materials (*saṃbhāra*), he offers a spoonful (*sruc-āhuti*) with the verse, "He has overcome all hostile armies" (4.2.8a,1). He causes the horse to step forward toward the east with its right forefoot upon the mound (*irmā*) with the formula, "That is the world of Agni" (ibid., to the end). Then, with the verse, "When you first neighed at birth" (4.2.8b,1), he makes it step back again in the same manner. And with the verse, "Rising from the ocean or from the soil—that is yours, O steed" (ibid., to the end)—he does so once more.
"Indraṃ viśvā avīvṛdhan... [He releases the horse]. With the verse "sam u... patiṃ," they hold it in front at the time for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
[The items are: the *kumbha*-bricks, the *caru*, the gold plate (*rukma*), and the golden man (*hiraṇyapuruṣa*).

The Adhvaryu takes the water-drawings (apāṃ grahāḥ) from outside the limit on the northern hip; the waters are there. Of them, he takes [the water] with two verses each, by means of pairs of jar-bricks, with the formulas: "O you who are worthy of sacrifice, you have come along the path" (KS 39.1:118.5; cf. ApŚS 16.32.5), and "I take you for the splendor of Agni, for the deities; you are pleasant, overcoming; for the Ādityas, the gods, [for their deities]. (K4,57a2) [End of citation]. (ApŚS reads *devatābhir*.)

I take you—ye are bright, full of vigor; from the deities of Indra, the possessor of power, I take you. (ibid. 118.7) Ye are sustainers of dominion, full of splendor; from the deities of the two gods Mitra and Varuṇa, I take you. (ibid. 118.15–16) Ye dwell in the fold, resting on high; from the deities of all the gods, I take you. (ibid. 118.13–14) Thou art the overlord, full of vigor; by the sacred word (*brahman*) of Bṛhaspati, I take you. (K4, 57a3)

"I take [the portions] from the deities" (KS 39.1:118.5;9;7;15–16;13–14;11–12; ApŚS 16.32.5–33.1)—thus they hold them as they have been taken. ... [He recites] the case-ending: "O Agni" (TS 5.5.6.1a).

With the formula, "You two are a refuge and you two are a shield," he places two of these bricks upon that very hip with the formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, I settle you two, full of sweetness; by that deity, sit firm like Aṅgiras! (as found in the same source to the end, omitting "for light" and the *T* mantra).

With the mantra, “You two are *ṛta* and you two are *satya*” (KS 39.1:118.7–8; ApŚS 16.33.1), he places two bricks on the right shoulder. With the mantra, “Sit down by the impulse of the god... [for the sake of sight for you two? (ibid., end; likely without *cakṣuṣe vām*?), and with the mantra, “You two are slayers of rivals and slayers of enemies” (KS 39.1:118.12–13, 1; ApŚS 16.33.1), he places two bricks on the right hip. With the mantra, “Sit down by the impulse of the god... [for the sake of offspring for you two (KS) or for the sake of semen for you two (Ap)]” (ibid., end; likely without *prajābhyo vām* or *retase vām* respectively, and including the *Taittirīya* mantra).

With the mantra, "And you two are slayers of Rākṣasas and slayers of those who bestow gifts" (KS 39.1:118.10–11; Ap 16.33.1), he places two [bricks] on the northern shoulder with the formula, "Of the god...

sit ye" (ibid., omitting *retase vām* in KS or *prajābhyo vām* in Ap, and including the *Taittirīya* mantra); and with the mantra, "And you two are the past and the future" (KS 39.1:118.14–15; Ap 16.33.1), he places two [bricks] to the south of the naturally perforated stone (*svayamātṛṇṇā*) with the formula, "Of the god... sit ye" (KS 39.1:118.16–17; Ap 16.33.1, likely omitting *varcase vām*, and including the *Taittirīya* mantra).
